title: Reports Read Right
eyebrow: Everything you pointed at is fixed, and one thing you could not have seen

actions.fyi: Nothing is waiting on you. One round of review by someone who did not write this is still owed, and I cannot be the one to do it.

content.label: The button, and where it lives now
content.lead: It was a bar stuck under the card. It is now one of the card's own facts.

before.caption: Before — a second box below the card, wider than it, with a seam between

after.caption: After — one card, with its report sitting beside where the comment count goes

blocks.label: Why it was outside
blocks.text: It was placed under the card on purpose, because a card's corners already carry its number, its type and its badges, and I did not want a collision. That was the wrong call: every card layout already has a line at the bottom for its own small facts, and the report belongs on it. It now inherits the card's hover and selection, which a separate box never could.

content.label: The report that told its story twice
content.lead: One list is the work list's own and moves; the other was typed once and froze.

rows: "Nothing left to start" with three unfinished
Says everything left is under way

rows.title: The typed copy is gone, not corrected
rows.note: A second list of the same work is wrong the morning after it is written. The page now carries one list, and it is the work list's own.

rows.title: The two lines at the top describe the whole board
rows.note: "Now" counts the live items it does not name instead of showing one of three as though it were the only one. "Next up" is about work nobody has started, and when there is none but plenty unfinished it says that, rather than a phrase that reads as done.

rows.title: A page cannot go back to two lists
rows.note: A report that reads a card is now refused if it types a count of steps or carries a section named as the step list. Both refusals are narrow: a measurement that happens to read "48 of 166", and a section about what a plan got wrong, are still allowed — one of your other pages has each.

content.label: The link, and the drawer
content.lead: One would not open; the other was unreadable in a way nobody had measured.

rows.title: A finished report now hands you a web link
rows.note: It was handing you a file on your disk, and your terminal gives a file to the editor before any browser sees it. The link now points at the running screen, which also means the page is rebuilt as it opens and is never older than the work list behind it. With the screen down it falls back to the file and says so.

rows.title: The report in the drawer has room, and its contents stays put
rows.note: The page ran edge to edge; it now sits inside the drawer's margin with a frame around it. The contents list was only ever pinned on a wide screen — a drawer is not one — so it scrolled away exactly where it was most useful.

blocks.title: The thing you could not have seen
blocks.text: Measuring the drawer turned up a fault that has been there since the drawer existed: the report page was three times wider than the drawer holding it, so the right-hand column of every table sat off-screen with only a thin sideways scrollbar to say so. The contents strip had no width limit and dragged the whole page out with it. Fixed in the same change, and the drawer now refuses to accept a page wider than itself.

shots.caption: The drawer scrolled to the very bottom: contents still on top, the table's cost column back on screen, and the page inset from both edges

content.label: What stops all of it coming back
content.lead: Nine new rules, each one switched off on purpose and watched fail before it was trusted.

rows: A report typing its own count or list of the work
The report gates, before the page is built
A report button drawn outside its card
The board screen check, against a real browser
The checklist losing its order, or the two top lines lying
A checklist line falling back to our own vocabulary
The page in the drawer touching an edge, losing its contents, or running off the side
The drawer check, against a real browser

blocks.label: All green
blocks.text: Both screen checks are green, the report gates hold at 34 of 34, and all 72 unit tests are green. Every one of the nine rules was seen red on its own fault first — a check that has never failed is not known to work.

decisions.title: A card's report is one of the card's own facts, not an attachment
decisions.why: It sits on the line the card already keeps for its comment and related counts, so it inherits hover and selection and can never drift away from the card again.

decisions.title: A report that reads the work list never writes its own copy of it
decisions.why: Two lists of the same work disagree within a day, and you cannot tell which one to believe. The refusals that enforce it are deliberately narrow — they catch a typed count and a typed step list, not every sentence with a number in it.

decisions.title: A finished report hands over a web link, not a file
decisions.why: A file goes to whatever program claims it, and on your machine that is the editor. A web link opens in the browser and rebuilds the page from the work list as it opens.

decisions.title: A checklist line says what the work is for, in your words
decisions.why: The list above used to read "Guard:" and "Verify:" followed by the goal's title over and over. Each line now names its purpose — reproduce it, decide the shape, build it, check that it works — and the goal's title is said once, at the top.

decisions.title: The drawer refuses a page wider than itself
decisions.why: A sideways scrollbar is invisible until you go looking, and it had been hiding the last column of every table on every report opened in a drawer.

next.if_nothing: Reports stay correct and the checks keep them that way; the one round of outside review stays owed.

steps.step: Someone who did not write this reviews it once
Every agent that owns a card hands over a report when it finishes a piece of work
Buttons on a report that write straight back to the work list
